description: Create, preserve, destroy in order to be reborn: Vishnu and Shiva, pillars of the Trimurti, keep the cyclical time of Hinduism turning.

hero.hook: One comes down to Earth to save order. The other dances to burn it all and start again. Together they keep the universe going.

blocks.text: In Hindu mythology, time is not a straight line. It is a series of cycles. At the top sits the [[Trimurti]]: three functions of one single principle. **Brahma** creates. **Vishnu** preserves. **Shiva** destroys so that renewal is possible.

This course follows Vishnu and Shiva, the two liveliest pillars of that trinity. Their attributes, their incarnations and their symbols show how Hinduism holds together life and death, order and transformation.

The many gods are faces of one ultimate reality called [[Brahman]]. The Trimurti gives it three useful forms. **Brahma** brings the universe into being at the start of each cycle. His role then stops, which is why he is little worshipped in India today.

blocks.caption: Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva: create, preserve, transform

blocks.text: **Vishnu** makes sure that order holds. **Shiva** destroys what is worn out or corrupt. That destruction is not an absolute evil: it clears the ground for a new cycle. A “day of Brahma” lasts billions of years. Nothing is really lost, and everything starts again.
A single “day of Brahma” (a Kalpa) lasts **4.32 billion** years, oddly close to the age of the Earth as modern science measures it.

sections.title: The Trimurti, three faces of one principle

blocks.text: **Vishnu** protects [[Dharma]], the moral and cosmic law. When evil threatens to win, he comes down to Earth as an **avatar**. The [[Dashavatar]] tradition counts ten of them, animal at first, then human.

blocks.caption: Krishna, avatar of Vishnu: wisdom, love and just war

blocks.text: Among them, King **Rama** stands for virtue, and **Krishna** for wisdom and divine love. Hinduism even took in the **Buddha** as the ninth avatar. The tenth, **Kalki**, will come on a white horse to close the dark age of the [[Kali Yuga]].
From the 1980s on, the pioneers of computing borrowed the word “avatar” for the figure that stands in for a user in a virtual world.

**Shiva** is the god of paradoxes: an ascetic covered in ash on Mount [[Kailash]], and yet the husband of **Parvati** and the father of **Ganesha**. He embodies the energy that transforms, above all through dance.

blocks.caption: Nataraja: Shiva dances between creation and destruction

blocks.text: In the form of **Nataraja**, “king of the dance,” he performs the **Tandava**. In one hand the [[damaru]] beats the rhythm of creation. In the other burns the fire of destruction. One foot crushes ignorance, while the other, raised, offers release. Change is the only constant.
At CERN, in Geneva, a statue of Nataraja given by India reminds particle physicists of that dance: the endless creation and destruction of the universe.

Vishnu gives structure and guides through his incarnations. Shiva sets free by breaking illusions and attachments. Together they turn [[Samsara and karma]] into a road rather than a prison: be reborn, act, move forward.

Out of this duality came **Vaishnavism** and **Shaivism**, currents that enrich each other rather than fight, especially around [[The Bhagavad Gita]]. In this vision, every ending prepares a departure.

The **Trimurti** brings the universe into balance: Brahma creates, Vishnu preserves through his avatars, Shiva destroys so that life can return. It is a cyclical vision in which karma and samsara make every destruction the opening of a new cycle.
